passage: Board exams were three months away, and Avni's parents had stopped her Kathak class to save money and time. But every night, after the dishes, she practised in the narrow corridor of their flat, ghungroos wrapped in a cloth so the neighbours wouldn't complain. Her friend Payal found her there at ten one night, sweat on her lip, counting beats under her breath. "Aren't you exhausted?" "Yes," Avni said. "But when I dance, I stop being tired inside." She had copied her teacher's compositions into a notebook and was teaching herself the next one. Payal watched her spin, feet muffled, and didn't say anything about the exams.

qa.q: Why were Avni's ghungroos wrapped in a cloth?
qa.a: So the neighbours wouldn't complain.

qa.q: What does "I stop being tired inside" reveal about Avni?
qa.a: Dance is deeply meaningful to her; it restores her emotionally even when she is physically exhausted.

qa.q: How could Avni protect both her passion and her exams?
qa.a: Keep a fixed, shorter dance slot each night after study, so dance stays a source of energy rather than a clash.

qa.q: Why might Payal have said nothing about the exams?
qa.a: Seeing how much dance meant to Avni, she may have decided a reminder would only hurt.

grounding: It shows a teenager's intense emotional investment in dance despite money and exam constraints.

passage: Wasim, sixteen, had turned the balcony of their Hyderabad flat into a small recovery corner for injured street dogs, with his mother's permission and a local vet's number stuck to the wall. He spent his pocket money on bandages and dog food. He made posters, ran an online group of forty volunteers, and once argued with the society secretary for an hour to let a limping puppy stay a week. His sister Minakshi teased him: "You'll marry a dog." But when a frightened mother dog finally let Wasim touch her, Minakshi saw his face, soft and fierce at once, and stopped teasing. At night he still sat up with the group chat, planning.

qa.q: How many volunteers were in Wasim's online group?
qa.a: Forty volunteers.

qa.q: What does Wasim's face, soft and fierce at once, suggest he felt when the mother dog let him touch her?
qa.a: Deep care and determination, showing how much this cause means to him.

qa.q: How could Wasim keep his passion from wearing him out?
qa.a: Share tasks with his volunteers and set some hours when he is off the group chat.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's view change?
qa.a: She moved from teasing him to respecting how much the cause meant to him.

grounding: It shows a teenager's strong drive and emotional investment in a cause he cares about.

passage:
"Ankita Didi, wake up! It's 3 a.m., the meteor shower's peaking."
"Sachin, go to sleep."
"I've waited since June. There might be sixty an hour. Come to the terrace, please."
Ankita groaned but followed, wrapped in a blanket. Sachin had already laid out two mats and a notebook.
"Why do you even care so much?" she mumbled.
"Because they're bits of a comet that passed long ago, and we're only seeing them now. Doesn't that give you goosebumps?"
A streak crossed the sky. Ankita gasped.
"That's one," Sachin whispered, writing it down. "Thirteen more and it's my best count ever."
"Fine," said Ankita. "I'll count the left side."

qa.q: At what time did Sachin wake Ankita?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: What does "Doesn't that give you goosebumps?" show about Sachin?
qa.a: He is emotionally moved by astronomy and wants others to feel the wonder he feels.

qa.q: How could Ankita support Sachin's passion beyond tonight?
qa.a: She might help him find an astronomy club or join him for the next sky event.

qa.q: How did Ankita's attitude shift during the night?
qa.a: She started out grumpy and sleepy, but after seeing a meteor she offered to count the left side. 😊

grounding: It shows a teenager's intense drive and emotional investment in astronomy, drawing his sister in.

passage: Last monsoon I found my grandfather's old valve radio in the storeroom, dead and covered in dust. I don't know why it grabbed me, but it did. For months I skipped cricket, spent my pocket money on second-hand parts from the electronics lane, and watched repair videos till my eyes burned. My friend Zainab said, "Nitin, you talk about capacitors the way other people talk about cricket scores." When the radio finally crackled into an old Hindi song one night in January, I actually cried a little. Looking back, it wasn't really about the radio. It was the feeling of caring about something so much that time disappeared. My marks dipped that term, and I had to fix that too. But now I repair radios for three neighbours, and I want to study electronics.

qa.q: Where did Nitin find the old radio?
qa.a: In the storeroom.

qa.q: Why did Nitin cry a little when the radio played?
qa.a: Months of intense effort had finally worked, and the moment meant a lot to Nitin.

qa.q: What could Nitin do to keep this passion without the marks dipping again?
qa.a: Nitin could set fixed repair hours around study time, perhaps with a parent or teacher helping to plan them.

qa.q: How does Zainab seem to see Nitin's passion?
qa.a: Zainab teases Nitin about it, but clearly noticed how deeply Nitin cared.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense emotional investment in a hobby that grows into a direction for study.

passage: Teacher's note, eco-club, October. Disha has changed since the neem tree near the back gate was marked for cutting to widen the parking. She has come to every club meeting early, with printouts about the birds that nest in it and a petition signed by 212 students. She drew the tree's canopy on chart paper and worked out how much of the Class 1 line it shades at noon. When Rajni suggested they plant saplings elsewhere instead, Disha's voice shook: 'Saplings won't shade anyone for twenty years.' She apologised later for snapping. Next step: I have arranged for Disha and Rajni to present both ideas together to the principal on Monday, and reminded Disha to get some sleep; she looks tired.

qa.q: How many students signed the petition?
qa.a: 212 students.

qa.q: Why did Disha's voice shake when Rajni suggested saplings?
qa.a: She cared intensely about saving the tree and felt the saplings idea missed what mattered to her.

qa.q: Why is presenting both ideas together a wise step?
qa.a: It channels Disha's energy into a fair proposal and protects her friendship with Rajni, while the teacher also watches her tiredness. 👍

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Disha snapped?
qa.a: Probably hurt or taken aback, since she was trying to help, though Disha's apology may have eased it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's intense drive for a cause, seen and gently guided by a teacher.

passage:
Thomas's diary, Saturday
Up at 5.30 again to catch Jupiter before the clouds came. Disha, my sister, says I'm obsessed. Maybe. I spent all my birthday money on the second-hand telescope, and now I can't stop. Tonight I saw four of Jupiter's moons, tiny dots in a line. My hands were shaking. I drew them in my notebook, then checked the chart: they match! I want to understand everything about how they move. Disha asked if I'd come to the mall tomorrow. I said maybe. Really I want to read about orbits. I don't know where this is going, but it feels like the most important thing I do.

qa.q: How many of Jupiter's moons did Thomas see?
qa.a: Four of Jupiter's moons.

qa.q: What does Thomas's hands shaking suggest?
qa.a: Thomas felt thrilled and deeply excited to see the moons through the telescope.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas as this passion grows?
qa.a: Look for an astronomy club or older mentor, and keep a balance with sleep and family time.

qa.q: How does Disha see Thomas's new passion?
qa.a: Disha thinks Thomas is obsessed, maybe with a mix of teasing and curiosity.

grounding: Shows a teenager developing an intense passion for astronomy.

passage: In the small town, Devika, sixteen, practised Bharatanatyam every morning before school on the flat roof, while the rest of the house slept. Her teacher Shalini had said she had the steps but not yet the feeling. So Devika watched old performances in the evenings and cried at one of them without knowing why. She started practising the facial expressions in front of the steel almirah's mirror. Her feet bled once. She didn't stop. When Shalini finally said, "Now you're telling the story," Devika felt her whole chest open. She wanted this more than anything.

qa.q: Where did Devika practise every morning?
qa.a: On the flat roof.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Shalini said she was telling the story?
qa.a: She felt overjoyed and moved, as if her whole chest opened.

qa.q: What would you advise Devika about her bleeding feet?
qa.a: Rest and have them looked at by an adult, since passion lasts longer when the body is cared for.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Devika's progress?
qa.a: With pride, seeing a student who went beyond steps to real feeling.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense emotional investment in classical dance.

passage: In Porto, Ines, fifteen, had turned her bedroom into a turtle headquarters. Maps of the coast were taped to the wall, with red pins where people had found turtles tangled in fishing nets. Every Saturday she cycled to the beach with her friend Astrid to pick up plastic, even in the rain. She wrote to three local councillors. Two didn't answer. She kept writing. When Astrid said, "You talk about turtles more than anything," Ines laughed, but her eyes were bright. "Because nobody else is." At the beach clean-up that week, forty people came, many of them from her school. Ines stood on a rock, handing out bags, grinning so hard her face hurt.

qa.q: How many people came to the beach clean-up?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling when she stood on the rock handing out bags?
qa.a: She felt joyful and proud, full of energy for the cause she loves.

qa.q: How could Ines keep her passion going without burning out?
qa.a: She could share tasks with others at the clean-ups and take breaks, so the cause isn't all on her.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Ines's passion?
qa.a: Astrid finds it intense but seems to admire it and keeps joining her.

grounding: A Portuguese teenager's passion for saving turtles drives her campaigns and clean-ups.

passage: The robotics lab at the Pune school closed at six, but Vidya was there until the guard came to switch off the lights. Her team's robot kept turning left when it should go straight. Mr Mridul, the teacher in charge, found her crouched over the motor again. "You've been here every evening this week." "It's so close, Sir." Her hands were greasy, and there was a pencil behind her ear. "When it works, it'll be the best feeling." He sat down. "Show me what you've tried." She explained six changes, one after another, eyes lit up. He pointed at one wire. She tightened it. The robot rolled straight across the floor. Vidya jumped up so fast she knocked over a chair.

qa.q: What time did the robotics lab close?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when the robot finally rolled straight?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and elated, jumping up so fast she knocked over a chair.

qa.q: What did Mr Mridul do that helped?
qa.a: He asked her to explain what she'd tried before pointing to the loose wire.

qa.q: How might Mr Mridul see Vidya staying late every evening?
qa.a: He seems impressed by her dedication, and perhaps a little concerned she's working too long.

grounding: A teenager's passion for robotics keeps her working late until her robot finally works.

passage:
Dear Wasim,
You asked why I didn't come to the cricket match. The truth is I was at tabla class, and then I stayed two more hours practising a new taal. I know you think it's strange. It's not just a hobby anymore. When Guruji plays, I feel like my whole chest is the drum. I've started waking at five to practise before school. I listen to recordings on the bus. My fingers have calluses. Some days I'm tired and frustrated and nothing sounds right, and I still can't stop. There's a youth concert in December. Guruji says I might play. Will you come? It would mean a lot.
Suraj

qa.q: What time has Suraj started waking to practise?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel when Guruji plays?
qa.a: Suraj feels deeply moved and alive, as if the whole chest is the drum.

qa.q: How could Suraj share this passion with Wasim?
qa.a: Suraj could invite Wasim to the youth concert, as the letter does, or to watch a practice session.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Wasim might feel surprised by how much tabla means to Suraj and glad to be invited.

grounding: A teenager writes to a friend about a growing passion for tabla.

passage:
Okay, Madhav, you're recording? Good. I'm Gargi, and this is about turtles.
In Class 8 we went on a beach clean-up in Chennai just to skip school. At five in the morning we saw volunteers guarding a nest with a torch. Tiny turtles scrambling for the water. I cried. In front of everyone.
Since then, I've done every night walk I'm allowed to. I made posters for our colony about switching off beach-facing lights. My mother says I talk about turtles at dinner so much the dal gets cold.
Some people think it's a phase. Maybe. But when I'm on the sand at night, I feel like the most useful version of myself.
This year I'm training juniors to do night walks too. That's my favourite part now.

qa.q: What did Gargi make posters about?
qa.a: Switching off beach-facing lights.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel during the night walks?
qa.a: Gargi feels purposeful and deeply moved, like the most useful version of Gargi.

qa.q: How could Gargi's parents support this passion?
qa.a: They can keep allowing the night walks with a responsible group and help Gargi balance them with sleep and school.

qa.q: How might Gargi's mother see this passion?
qa.a: Gargi's mother teases about cold dal but probably feels proud of how much Gargi cares.

grounding: Shows a teen developing an intense, lasting commitment to a conservation cause.

passage:
I'm Lakshmi, Zeenat's neighbour. She's been drawing comics since the summer holidays, and now it's taken over.
At first it was a notebook on the steps. Then she bought cheap ink pens with her pocket money. Now she's on our shared staircase every evening, with pages spread out and a torch when the bulb goes.
Last week her mother called her three times for dinner. Zeenat said, "One panel more, Ammi," three times.
She showed me a page once. It was about a girl who sells chai at a railway station. It was good. Really good.
I don't know if she'll become an artist. But when she's drawing, her whole face changes, like she's somewhere else.

qa.q: Where does Zeenat draw every evening?
qa.a: On the shared staircase, with pages spread out and a torch when the bulb goes.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's face while drawing suggest about Zeenat's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she feels absorbed and happy, as if lost in something she loves.

qa.q: How could Zeenat's mother help her balance the comics and dinner?
qa.a: She could agree on a time to stop and show interest in the pages, so Zeenat feels supported, not blocked.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Zeenat's drawing?
qa.a: Lakshmi thinks the work is really good and sees Zeenat change while drawing, though she doesn't know where it will lead.

grounding: A neighbour describes a teen's growing, all-absorbing passion for drawing comics.

passage:
First week of June: Mohit heard a debate on the radio about the new flyover cutting down old trees on his road. He didn't care much. Trees were trees.
Two weeks later: the axes started. His neighbour Salma aunty stood crying near the gulmohar that had shaded her shop for thirty years. Mohit watched, fists in pockets, and felt something shift.
By August: he had joined a citizens' group, learned the names of every tree on the road, and was spending weekends with a measuring tape and a register. His mother complained his room smelt of paper and mud.
One Sunday he spoke at a small meeting, voice trembling. Afterwards Salma aunty patted his cheek. "You care more than I did at your age," she said.

qa.q: Which tree had shaded Salma aunty's shop?
qa.a: The gulmohar, for thirty years.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel watching the axes?
qa.a: He felt upset and angry, standing with fists in his pockets as something shifted in him.

qa.q: What could help Mohit keep his passion going without burning out?
qa.a: Sharing tasks with the citizens' group and keeping time for rest and school would help him last.

qa.q: How might Salma aunty feel about Mohit's efforts?
qa.a: Salma aunty seems touched and grateful, patting his cheek and saying he cares more than she did at his age.

grounding: Tracks a teen's growing commitment to saving trees over a summer.

passage: Afreen, beti, you asked why your old Divyansh Uncle from accounts spends every weekend at the lake. When I was fifteen, the lake behind our Bhopal colony was turning into a dump. One morning I found a heron tangled in a plastic net, and I couldn't stop thinking about it. I started counting birds every dawn before school, in a notebook with a torn cover. I wrote to the municipal office, got no answer, and wrote again. I dragged my friend Qadir to clean the bank every Sunday for a year. My marks slipped that term, and my mother was furious. But when the corporation finally put up a fence and bins, I cried on the bank like a fool. I still have that notebook: 812 herons counted.

qa.q: What did young Divyansh find tangled in a plastic net?
qa.a: A heron.

qa.q: How did young Divyansh feel when the corporation put up the fence and bins?
qa.a: Divyansh felt overwhelmed with relief and joy, crying on the bank after a year of effort.

qa.q: Which choice kept the lake campaign alive after the first letter got no answer?
qa.a: Writing again and cleaning the bank every Sunday for a year kept the pressure on, even when nothing seemed to change.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's mother see the lake work that term?
qa.a: Divyansh's mother was furious when the marks slipped, seeing the lake work as a distraction from school.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense, lasting drive to protect a lake, told by a senior colleague as a memory.
